editorial.headline: Designing the Domestic Objects We Live With—and Bali’s PMA Divide
editorial.standfirst: This industrial-design activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet PMA registration for it is blocked in Bali today.
editorial.body:
This activity is industrial design for household equipment and furniture: the product-design work behind the objects that furnish, equip and decorate domestic life. Its scope runs from glassware, tableware, cookware and food-storage items to fireplace accessories, beds, tables, chairs and storage furniture. It also includes mirrors and frames, clothes hangers, curtains and blinds, wall and table ornaments, vases and pots, medals and belts, flags and festival decorations, and artificial flowers, fruit and plants. The work may be carried out through specialist software. Taken together, the scope is about designing the products themselves across a broad domestic and furnishing landscape.

Nationally, the activity is open to PMA, with a foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. It is available at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales, so the classification accommodates work ranging from the smallest operating scale through to large business. That national position matters: it states plainly that foreign ownership is not capped below full ownership for this activity at the national level. The reference cited for that position is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021.

Bali, however, produces a different registration outcome. A foreign-owned business cannot register this activity in Bali today. The Bali record marks it as blocked under its risk-class rule because, at the Besar scale, every scope is assessed in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk. Bali’s province-wide, permanent moratorium blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities; for this activity, that rule has applied since May 13, 2026. This is not a lower foreign-ownership ceiling in Bali: it is a block on PMA registration. Founders should therefore read the national 100% ceiling and the Bali outcome together—the activity is fully foreign-open nationally, but unavailable for PMA registration in Bali under the recorded moratorium.
